module_title: Field Applications, Particle Kinematics & Parallel Wires (Intermediate)
introduction: This level focuses on the rigorous mathematical derivation and application of Biot-Savart and Ampere's laws for standard geometries (wires, coils, solenoids). It also explores the complex kinematics of charged particles moving in magnetic fields (circular and helical trajectories).

core_concepts.title: Magnetic Field due to Standard Geometries
core_concepts.description:
1. Straight infinitely long wire: $B = \frac{\mu_0 I}{2\pi r}$. 
2. Center of a circular coil: $B = \frac{\mu_0 N I}{2 R}$ (where $N$ is turns). 
3. On the axis of a circular coil at distance $x$: $B = \frac{\mu_0 N I R^2}{2(R^2 + x^2)^{3/2}}$. 
4. Ideal long Solenoid (inside): $B = \mu_0 n I$ (where $n = N/L$ is turns per unit length). The field outside an ideal solenoid is zero.

core_concepts.title: Motion of a Charged Particle in a Uniform Magnetic Field
core_concepts.description:
If $\vec{v}$ is perpendicular to $\vec{B}$ ($\theta = 90^\circ$), the particle undergoes Uniform Circular Motion. The magnetic force provides the necessary centripetal force ($qvB = mv^2/r$). 
Radius: $r = \frac{mv}{qB} = \frac{p}{qB} = \frac{\sqrt{2mK}}{qB}$ (where $K$ is kinetic energy). 
Time Period: $T = \frac{2\pi m}{qB}$. Note that $T$ is completely independent of the velocity ($v$) or radius ($r$).

core_concepts.title: Helical Motion
core_concepts.description: If the velocity vector $\vec{v}$ makes an arbitrary angle $\theta$ (other than $0^\circ, 90^\circ, 180^\circ$) with $\vec{B}$, the velocity resolves into $v_{\perp} = v \sin\theta$ (causes circular motion) and $v_{\parallel} = v \cos\theta$ (causes linear motion). The resulting path is a Helix. The linear distance traveled in one full rotation is called the Pitch: $P = v_{\parallel} T = (v \cos\theta) \frac{2\pi m}{qB}$.

core_concepts.title: Force Between Two Parallel Current-Carrying Wires
core_concepts.description: Two parallel infinite wires separated by distance $d$ carrying currents $I_1$ and $I_2$ exert a magnetic force on each other. The force per unit length is $F/L = \frac{\mu_0 I_1 I_2}{2\pi d}$. This forms the operational definition of the standard unit 'Ampere'.

important_entities.name: The Cyclotron Frequency
important_entities.significance: Because the time period of a charged particle in a magnetic field is independent of its speed, devices like Cyclotrons can accelerate particles continuously using a constant-frequency alternating electric field synced perfectly with this magnetic rotation.

trap_alerts_and_exceptions.explanation: In electrostatics, 'like charges repel, unlike attract'. In magnetism of parallel wires, it is the EXACT OPPOSITE. Wires carrying currents in the SAME direction ATTRACT each other. Wires carrying currents in OPPOSITE directions REPEL each other. Do not confuse this with electrostatic rules.

mnemonics_and_tricks.explanation: In many JEE/NEET questions, particles (alpha, proton, electron) are accelerated through the same potential difference $V$. Since Kinetic Energy $K = qV$, you can instantly find the radius ratio using $r = \frac{\sqrt{2m(qV)}}{qB} = \sqrt{\frac{2mV}{qB^2}}$. Thus, $r \propto \sqrt{m/q}$.

exam_strategy_tips: For problems involving a wire bent into multiple segments (e.g., straight parts and semicircles), use the Principle of Superposition. Calculate the magnitude and direction (using $\odot$ for out of page, $\otimes$ for into page) for each segment separately and add them as vectors.
